209.history: The great Tuathaich gathering-village is Martha Greaves's town and Ellen Marsh's. The fuel was shown burning in its mill yard in the second year. Agnes Pike's school gave its schoolroom to the binders of Tional nan Tuathach's books and its back room to Ellen Marsh's gathering of Sceulachdan nan Tuathach, eleven books from {{year:VI-0058}}, whose keeping at the library was asked and laid on the table. Tional nan Tuathach's wool mills bought the holdouts' coal, and in the twentieth year its granaries stood fuller than the five years' average by half again, the autumn entry giving no reason. In the war Agnes Pike's school was given over to families of the western hills, near sixty souls on its benches, and Ellen Marsh began a twelfth book of their telling. Martha Greaves went home to Doire ghlas when she laid down the chair. In the present year An t-Aon Leabhar Deug go from school to school to be copied, and on the shortest evening Ellen Marsh told the eldest children the telling of A' Chiad Churach.
209.known_for: Agnes Pike's school, An t-Aon Leabhar Deug, and Tional nan Tuathach's granaries

338.history: The small eastern town of An dàrna rèisimeid's garrison was quiet until the war. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, who had been royal chronicler since before Linn an Dubhain, laid down the office in {{year:VI-0074}} and went there to live, and watched An dàrna rèisimeid's camp being pitched from her garden wall when it was raised in the autumn of the war's first year, writing to Sìleas nic Rath of it. The regiment guards Slighe a' Ghuail and the library road. She died at Àth dhìreach in {{year:VI-0144}}. The town is small, a street of houses on Slighe a' Ghuail's embankment and the regiment's camp on the water-meadow below it. The camp's first winter was spent under canvas; its huts went up the next spring from timber brought by Slighe a' Ghuail, and the town's one inn has taken the regiment's custom since.
338.known_for: An dàrna rèisimeid, and the old chronicler's last years

26.history: The deep-water harbour beside the capital sent Anna nic Phàil to the council. As its councillor she gave the speaker of Tional nan Tuathach the smallest incline of the head across the council table when Athchuinge Dheireannach an Tionail was carried in, and in {{year:VI-0137}} she brought Tagradh na h-Èirig to the western towns, cutting a page of figures from her own draft before she laid it. The motion was held over morning after morning and let lie. The harbour is deep enough for the tank-hulls, and the dubhan for the capital's lamp-houses comes in there from the southern works by sea, in hulls of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein, to be carted the short road to Cathair dhearg; the town's carters did well in the war, when the lamp-houses were rationed but the tanks were not.
26.known_for: Anna nic Phàil's Tagradh na h-Èirig
